articles.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
articles.summary: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.
articles.content:
A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes.

There’s little left of the ship itself but based on clues from its cargo – including pottery vessels – a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 BCE.

That’s about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world’s oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago.

Much work remains to be done to finesse the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age.

Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today.

Searching for clues

Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks.

Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck.

As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, this was a singular experience. New technology, water-logged methods of excavation and laborious conservation techniques were the new normal. Yet there is always room for learning new skills in life.

Of the ship itself there is now nothing to see, owing to underwater exposure. Yet the research team has now estimated the ship and its cargo dates to around 2700–2400 BCE. However, the precise dating is still under consideration. Earlier or later dates on either side of this initial determination are also possible.

A time capsule of ancient trade

This discovery promises to re-write our understanding of early trade networks from around 4,500 years ago.

The ship is a “missing piece” in the story of networks, trade and commodity exchange in the wider eastern Mediterranean. This era includes the pyramid age of Giza and its mighty pharaohs.

What remains under the sea is a time capsule of ancient trade.

Although its direction was not known, the boat was evidently traveling along the coast of southern Turkey.

Now resting on the seabed between two islands, it is apparent the ship likely sought refuge in the lee waters during a storm. One could imagine the terror of the sailors – possibly coastal people from the Levant region – as their ship crashed against the rocks.

While timbers from the ship disappeared long ago, the remains of its precious cargo were embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast.

Divers worked over the past four months to extract its pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope.

A closer look at pottery

Pottery is like plastic: it never goes away and just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.

Yet humble pottery vessels hold many clues about the past.

In this case, the cargo included large ceramic storage vessels or amphorae which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.

The pots were large ovoid, flat-based jars with two handles, many featuring a raised horizontal clay “belt” around the widest part of the jar.

Through these vessels was possible to ascertain many pieces of information. This includes the likely origin of the jars and the contents exchanged across the region.

Importantly, the shape and manufacturing technique of the pots themselves help us date the cargo. By extension, this includes also the date of other pottery, and the ship itself.

The bigger picture

Compared to later periods, trade and exchange in the eastern Mediterranean during the third millennium (3000–2000 BCE) is poorly understood.

Maritime voyages during the that period are known from Egyptian texts, pottery vessels and raw materials from ancient tombs.

Around the same time as this ship struck the rocks, the ancient Egyptians were trading in the eastern Mediterranean through the port of Byblos in Lebanon.

Commodities such as cedar, tin/lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli and silver, all materials that Egypt lacked, were imported by the Egyptian state.

Recent scientific research also reveals that silver was acquired by the Egyptian state around 2600 BCE. Analyses showed this silver was acquired from the Lavrion mines east of modern Athens.

While it is unlikely Egyptian ships made this journey, boats like the Kekova ship may have used the route as part of an extended international maritime network.

And what was in the jars? Remarkably there were still residues visible to the naked eye. Again, scientific analyses are pending, but could be some of the products mentioned in the Egyptian texts, possibly olive oil, wine or tree resin.

The ship may have acquired its pottery from several ports on their journey. Our best assessment at this stage of research is that some of the “belted” jars (or clays used to make them) may have originated in the Central Jordan Valley.

The coast of southern Turkey is littered with ancient shipwrecks. While maritime archaeology is a relatively recent phenomenon, some of the world’s most famous wrecks have been discovered there. Who knows what other secrets these waters hold.

The research on which this article is based was led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, head of the Division of Mediterranean Underwater Cultural Heritage Research, and the Department of Restoration and Conservation of Cultural Heritage in the Faculty of Art at the Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey.

articles.personality_title: Archaeologists discover world's oldest shipwreck off Turkey's coast
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Archaeologists have long studied ancient shipwrecks to learn about early trade. The oldest known shipwreck before this discovery was found near Greece and is about 4,200 years old. 

**What happened** – In 2024, a team led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz found a shipwreck off the coast of Kekova, Turkey. The wooden ship itself has disappeared, but pottery found at the site helped date the wreck to about 4,500 years ago, making it possibly the oldest shipwreck ever found. The ship likely crashed during a storm while carrying goods like oil, wine, or tree resin.

**Impact** – This discovery gives new information about trade in the ancient Mediterranean Sea during the Early Bronze Age. It shows that people were connected by sea and exchanged valuable goods far earlier than previously known. The pottery tells us about the materials traded and shows links between places like the Jordan Valley and Egypt at the time of the Egyptian pyramids.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue studying the pottery and any residues inside to learn exactly what the ship carried. They will also work to confirm the dating and publish their findings in scientific journals. This could change how historians understand early maritime trade routes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A 4,500-year-old shipwreck found off Turkey reveals new details about ancient Mediterranean trade and connections during the time of the Egyptian pyramids.

articles.personality_title_es: Arqueólogos descubren el naufragio más antiguo del mundo frente a la costa de Turquía
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los arqueólogos han estudiado naufragios antiguos para aprender sobre el comercio temprano. El naufragio más antiguo conocido antes de este hallazgo estaba cerca de Grecia y tiene unos 4,200 años.

**Qué pasó** – En 2024, un equipo dirigido por el profesor asociado Hakan Öniz encontró un naufragio frente a Kekova, Turquía. El barco de madera ya no se conserva, pero la cerámica encontrada permitió fechar el naufragio en aproximadamente 4,500 años, lo que podría ser el más antiguo del mundo. El barco probablemente naufragó durante una tormenta mientras transportaba productos como aceite, vino o resina.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento aporta nueva información sobre el comercio en el Mediterráneo antiguo durante la Edad del Bronce Temprano. Muestra que las personas estaban conectadas por mar y comerciaban bienes valiosos mucho antes de lo que se creía. La cerámica revela los materiales intercambiados y las conexiones entre lugares como el Valle del Jordán y Egipto en la época de las pirámides.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando la cerámica y los residuos para saber qué llevaba el barco. También confirmarán la fecha y publicarán sus resultados en revistas científicas. Esto podría cambiar cómo los historiadores entienden las primeras rutas comerciales marítimas.

**Una frase clave** – Un naufragio de 4,500 años descubierto frente a Turquía revela nuevos detalles sobre el comercio mediterráneo antiguo en la época de las pirámides egipcias.

articles.title: New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and […]
The post New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and delight them, and that they had no intention of seeking out.

NJ Transit has been doing this since 2019, when it launched the TRANSITional Art Project as a pilot at Newark Penn Station. Working with the New Jersey State Council on the Arts, it has since installed temporary exhibitions of murals and photography by New Jersey artists at seven more stations. The latest is now at Morris Plains Rail Station: a show called “Tracks Through Time: Movement, History and Human Connection.”

A show about the tracks themselves

The subject matter has good timing. The exhibition looks at 250 years of American history through the lens of railroads, in the very stations where people still depend on those rails to get to work. It includes photography by Beyti Barbaros, murals by Jonathan Yumi, and a three-panel mural installation by Catherine Thurston.

“Railroads helped to build this nation,” said NJ Transit President and CEO Kris Kolluri, “and as we mark 250 years of our shared history, there’s no better place to tell that story than in the very stations where the past and daily life intersect.”

Art you don’t have to go looking for

Nobody goes to a train station specifically to see art, but that might be at the heart of the reasoning for this whole project. Most people at a gallery already decided they wanted to be there. The commuter who glances up at a mural while waiting for the 8:14 didn’t, and that’s a different kind of encounter.

Danielle Bursk, the New Jersey State Arts Council Director of Community Partnerships & Artist Services, put it this way: “Public art has the power to transform the places we move through every day into places where we can pause, connect, and see our communities in new ways.”

The program also pays the artists. Some participants receive stipends toward the cost of developing a project in a transit space, which matters given how rarely public art comes with any budget at all.

The program has now reached eight stations: Newark, Camden, Atlantic City, Trenton, New Brunswick, Summit, Rahway, and Morris Plains.
